sum: What code review is actually for, how to write a change that's easy to review and a review that improves it, what to look for in what order, feedback that lands, keeping review fast — with Google's data on 9 million reviews and Apple's 'goto fail' as the bug a reviewer should catch.
prereq: swe1
Cohesion, coupling and SOLID give reviewers a vocabulary for design problems: one reason to change, narrow interfaces, dependencies pointing at policy.
swe4
Clean code and error handling: intention-revealing names, guard clauses, and never swallowing exceptions — the most common readability and correctness comments in review.
swe5
Tests at the right level, doubles that don't lie, and deterministic tests; a reviewer checks that the change's tests would fail if the behaviour broke.
why:
Two reviews of the same pull request. The first reviewer leaves 38 comments: rename this variable, add a blank line there, prefer a list comprehension, this docstring has a typo. The author spends a day addressing them, resentfully. Nobody notices that the new endpoint returns another customer's invoice if you change the ID in the URL, because the ownership check was never written. The second reviewer leaves four comments. One is marked blocking: "This endpoint loads the invoice by ID without checking it belongs to the caller — anyone can read any invoice. Could we scope the query by customer_id, and add a test that a different customer gets 404?" Two are suggestions with reasons. One says the retry logic is nicely done. The change merges the same afternoon, safer.

Code review is one of the few practices nearly every software team shares, and one of the most variable in quality. Done badly, it's a bottleneck that adds days of latency, a venue for style arguments, and a ritual that approves what nobody read. Done well, it catches the defects tests miss, spreads knowledge of the system across the team, keeps a codebase coherent as dozens of people change it, and is the main way engineers learn from each other. The difference is rarely talent; it's a set of learnable habits on both sides of the review.

This lesson covers those habits: what review is actually for, backed by Google's published study of nine million reviewed changes; how authors make changes easy to review, including splitting large work into stacks of small changes; what reviewers look for, in what order, and what they should leave to tools; how to write feedback that lands and handle disagreement; and how to keep review fast. The case study is Apple's 2014 "goto fail" bug — one duplicated line in the code that verifies secure connections, which silently disabled a crucial check on hundreds of millions of devices, and which is the canonical example of what a careful read of a diff can catch. The lab builds a tiny review bot that flags the same shape of bug automatically. Because this is an AI-engineering track, it also covers reviewing changes that aren't code in the usual sense: prompts, model versions and evaluation results.
primer:
The analogy: a co-pilot's cross-check

In a cockpit, the pilot flying sets the altimeter or enters a route, and the co-pilot independently checks it and calls it out. The check isn't an insult to the pilot's skill; it's a system that assumes anyone can make a slip, and it works because it's routine, quick and focused on what matters — altitude, heading, fuel — not on how neatly the pilot wrote the flight plan. Both pilots also learn from each other's habits over thousands of flights. Code review is the same cross-check: routine, focused, fast, and a source of shared knowledge.

The analogy breaks on timing. A co-pilot's check takes seconds and happens in the moment; a code review is asynchronous, and a check that waits two days in someone's queue has a real cost — the author has moved on, context is lost, and changes pile up. Speed is part of the practice, not an afterthought.

What review is for

Ask engineers why they review code and "finding bugs" comes first. It's real, but the evidence says review does several jobs at once. Google's 2018 study of its own review process — interviews, a survey, and logs of about 9 million reviewed changes by more than 25,000 engineers — found reviewers doing education (teaching and learning the codebase and conventions), maintaining norms (consistency and readability), gatekeeping (owners of code seeing changes to it), and accident prevention (catching bugs and design mistakes). The educational effect showed up in the data: engineers in their first year received more than twice as many comments per change as experienced ones, and the number of files engineers had seen through review grew steadily with seniority.

The lifecycle of a change

A change's path from idea to production has a few steps, and most of the leverage is in the early ones:

Notice where the leverage is. By the time a human reviewer opens the diff, three things should already be settled: the change is small enough to read carefully in one sitting, its description tells the reviewer what to look for, and every mechanical question — formatting, lint, types, whether the tests pass — has been answered by a machine. A reviewer who has to reconstruct the intent of a 1,400-line change from its code, or who spends the first twenty minutes on indentation, has been set up to miss the one line that matters. Most bad reviews are caused upstream of the reviewer.

A change is usually submitted as a pull request (PR) — also called a merge request, or at Google a changelist (CL): the diff, a description, and a discussion thread. The author writes and describes it; one or more reviewers read it and comment; the author iterates; a reviewer approves ("LGTM", looks good to me); the change merges. Everything that follows is about making each step cheap and effective: authors doing the work that makes review easy, tools doing the work that doesn't need a human, and reviewers spending their attention where it matters most.
body:
1. The author's job: small, single-purpose, well described

The most effective review improvement is made before anyone reviews: making the change small. Review quality drops as size rises — reviewers skim, useful comments per line fall, and latency grows — and a small change can be reverted on its own if it breaks something. Google's numbers show what "small" means in a healthy process: across roughly 9 million changes, the median modified 24 lines, over 35% touched a single file, and about 90% touched fewer than 10 files. That's not because Google's features are small; it's because features are delivered as sequences of small changes.

Three rules keep changes small and reviewable. One purpose per change: a refactor that changes no behaviour, a behaviour change, a dependency upgrade and a formatting sweep are four changes, because a reviewer reads each differently — a pure refactor is checked for "nothing changed", a behaviour change for "the right thing changed". Separate mechanical from meaningful: a rename touching 80 files goes in its own change, clearly labelled, so the 30-line logic change isn't hidden in it. Stack dependent work: when a feature needs several steps, submit them as a stack of small changes, each reviewable and mergeable on its own.

The description does half the reviewer's orientation. A good one answers five questions: what changes (one or two sentences), why (the problem or ticket, and why this approach over alternatives), how it was tested (tests added, manual checks, evaluation results), risk (what could break, who's affected), and rollback (revert safely? behind a flag?). For UI changes add screenshots; for performance changes, before-and-after numbers; for prompt or model changes, evaluation results.

Self-review is the cheapest review there is: read your own diff in the review tool, as a reviewer would, before asking anyone. Authors routinely catch debugging leftovers, commented-out code, missing tests, and accidental changes this way. Leave comments on your own diff where a reviewer will need context ("this looks redundant but X relies on it").

2. Let machines do what machines can

Every comment a tool could have made is wasted human attention and a source of friction. Before human review, CI should run a formatter (Black or Ruff's formatter — formatting is then not a topic), a linter (Ruff: unused imports, bare except, mutable default arguments, complexity), a type checker (mypy or pyright), the tests, and scanners for secrets and known-vulnerable dependencies. Automated review comments can also flag things like unreachable code, which, as the case study shows, is sometimes a critical bug. The rule: if a comment could be written by a rule, write the rule instead, once.

3. The reviewer's job: attention in order of importance

Review time is limited, so spend it in order of what costs most if missed. A practical sequence:

  1. Is this the right change? Read the description first. Does the change solve the stated problem? Is the approach sound, or is there a simpler design? Does the code belong in this module (swe1)? A design problem found here saves the author polishing code that will be rewritten; if the design is wrong, say so first and stop — line comments can wait.
  2. Is it correct? Edge cases (empty input, zero, maximum sizes, unicode), error paths (swe4), concurrency — two requests at once, retries, ordering (swe12) — and compatibility: will this work while old and new versions run side by side during a deploy? Will this migration lock a large table?
  3. Do the tests prove it? Would the new tests fail if the behaviour were wrong? Do they assert outcomes, cover the error paths, avoid timing and order dependence (swe5)? Is there a test for the bug being fixed?
  4. Is it secure and operable? Authorisation on every data access, input validation, secrets out of code, sensitive data out of logs (swe13); timeouts on external calls, useful logs and metrics, a way to roll back or turn it off.
  5. Is it readable? Names, function size, comments explaining why (swe4). Important, but last, and mostly suggestions rather than blockers.

Two habits make the sequence work. Read the tests early — they're the author's statement of intended behaviour, and gaps in them point to gaps in thinking. And read the whole diff, line by line, for anything that controls security or money. The case study is a single line.

4. A worked review

Here's a small diff adding an endpoint that returns an invoice, and a review of it.

+@app.get("/invoices/{invoice_id}")
+def get_invoice(invoice_id: int, user: User = Depends(current_user)):
+    try:
+        inv = db.query(Invoice).get(invoice_id)
+    except Exception:
+        return {"error": "not found"}
+    return inv.to_dict()

A focused review, using labels in the style of conventional comments (a label plus whether it blocks):

  • issue (blocking): "This loads any invoice by ID and never checks it belongs to user, so any logged-in user can read any invoice by changing the number. Could we query with customer_id=user.customer_id and return 404 when it doesn't match? And a test that another customer gets 404."
  • issue (blocking): "except Exception turns a database outage into a 'not found' with status 200. .get() returns None when there's no row, so we can drop the try, check for None and raise HTTPException(404); let real errors reach the error handler."
  • question: "Does to_dict() include the internal fraud_score field? If so we probably don't want it in the response — maybe a response model with explicit fields?"
  • praise: "Nice use of the current_user dependency — keeps auth consistent with the other routes."

Four comments, two blocking, each with a reason and a concrete suggestion, the most serious first. No comments on naming, since nothing was confusing. The reviewer found the two defects that matter by asking the step-2 and step-4 questions: what if the caller isn't the owner? and what happens when the database is down?

5. Writing feedback that lands

A review comment's job is to change the code, and that depends on the author accepting it. The practices that help are simple and consistently effective:

  • Comment on the code, not the person. "This function reads the balance and writes it back without a lock" rather than "you forgot about concurrency".
  • Explain why. "Prefer X" teaches nothing and invites argument; "X, because under two concurrent requests this read-then-write loses an update" teaches and persuades.
  • Label severity. Authors can't read minds: say what blocks merging and what's a take-it-or-leave-it nit. Conventional comments (issue, suggestion, question, nit, praise, with (blocking) or (non-blocking)) make this explicit.
  • Ask when you're unsure. "What happens if the list is empty here?" is honest when you don't know, and invites the author to explain or discover the bug themselves.
  • Say it once. If a pattern repeats, comment once and note "same in 6 other places", rather than 7 identical comments.
  • Note what's good. Specific praise ("the retry wrapper is cleanly separated") reinforces practices you want repeated and makes the critical comments easier to receive.
  • Escalate the medium, not the tone. After two rounds of back-and-forth on the same point, talk — a five-minute call resolves what twenty comments won't.

6. Receiving feedback, and disagreement

For authors, the useful stance is that comments are about the code and the reviewer is on the same side. Reply to every comment — with a fix, a question, or a reasoned disagreement — so the reviewer knows it was seen. Don't take nits personally; accept cheap ones even if you mildly prefer your version, and save your disagreement for things that matter. When you disagree, bring evidence (a benchmark, a link to the team standard, a failing case) rather than repeating your position. If a disagreement is purely taste and there's no team rule, defer to the code's owner, and if it keeps recurring, propose a rule so it's decided once. If it's substantive and unresolved, write down both options and ask a tech lead — a decision recorded in an architecture decision record (swe15) stops it being relitigated in every review.

7. Speed: review latency is a team metric

Slow review is expensive in ways that don't show up on a dashboard: authors context-switch to other work, changes pile up and conflict, and the temptation grows to batch changes into large PRs — which are slower to review, which makes the problem worse. Google's study found the median time from sending a change for review to approval was under four hours across all sizes, with a median wait for first feedback under an hour for small changes, and over 80% of changes needing at most one round of revisions; 70% of changes were committed within 24 hours of being sent. That speed comes from habits, not heroics: small changes, style automated away, and a norm that responding to a review takes priority over starting new work. Google's public guidance sets one business day as the maximum for a first response. Useful team measures are time to first review, time to approval, rounds per change and change size — not comment counts, which reward nitpicking.

Reviewer count matters too. At Google, the median change had exactly one reviewer, fewer than 25% had more than one — typically because a second approval was needed for ownership of files in another area. One knowledgeable reviewer who reads carefully beats three who each assume another read carefully.

8. Reviewing what isn't ordinary code

Some changes need a different lens. Schema migrations: will they lock a large table, and are they compatible with the version currently running (expand–contract, swe9)? Configuration and infrastructure: a one-line config change can take down every service; ask what the blast radius is and how it rolls out. Dependency upgrades: read the changelog for breaking changes and check the lockfile diff is what you expect. Deletions: is anything still calling this? And, increasingly, prompts and model configuration. A prompt template is behaviour: a changed instruction can shift outputs across every request. Keep prompts in version-controlled files so diffs are readable, require evaluation results in the description (the standard evaluation set, old versus new, with examples of changed outputs), check cost and latency effects, and make sure the change is versioned or behind a flag so it can be rolled back. "It looked better on the three examples I tried" is the prompt equivalent of "it works on my machine".

9. A reviewer's checklist for ML and LLM code

Machine-learning code has failure modes that ordinary review habits miss, so it's worth a few extra questions. Leakage: does any feature, normalisation statistic or tokenizer vocabulary get computed on data that includes the test set (ml9)? Train–serve consistency: is preprocessing shared between training and serving code, or duplicated so that it can drift (ml14)? Seeds and determinism: can the result be reproduced? Silent shape and dtype changes: a broadcast that turns a (32,) vector into a (32, 32) matrix trains without error and produces nonsense. Untrusted model output: is every model response parsed and validated before it reaches business logic or a database (swe4)? Cost: does the change add a model call inside a loop, multiplying spend and latency? And evaluation: is there evidence, on a fixed evaluation set, that the change helps — and is that set itself unchanged in this PR? None of these needs deep ML expertise to ask; all of them catch real incidents.

10. Beyond review: collaboration that makes review easier

Code review is late in the process; some problems are cheaper to catch earlier. A design review of a short document before a large change (swe15) catches wrong approaches before hundreds of lines are written. Pair programming — two people, one keyboard — is continuous review, and for tricky or unfamiliar code often faster than write-then-review. Ownership files (CODEOWNERS) route changes to people who know an area and make responsibility explicit. And team conventions written down — a style guide, a list of what reviewers look for, comment labels — turn review from personal preference into shared practice, which is what lets it scale.
deep:
What the research says review actually finds

Studies of review at Microsoft, Google and in open source converge on a picture that surprises people who think of review as bug-hunting. A large share of review comments concern maintainability — naming, structure, documentation, simpler alternatives — rather than functional defects, and reviewers who know the code well give markedly more useful comments than those who don't. That has practical consequences. Reviewer selection matters more than reviewer count: route changes to people who have recently edited or reviewed the same files (Google's tool does exactly this). Defect detection is strongest on small changes and falls off sharply with size. And because review is a relatively weak detector of deep functional bugs, it should be one layer among several — types, tests, static analysis, staged rollout — not the primary defence. The Google paper also found review is valued for "accident prevention" and "gatekeeping" even when few defects are found, because the knowledge that someone else will read the code changes how carefully it's written.

Ownership and readability: Google's two gates

Google's process has two explicit requirements beyond "someone approved it". Ownership: every directory has owners listed in a file, and a change needs approval from an owner of each affected directory, so the people accountable for an area see every change to it. Readability: a certification, per language, that an engineer writes idiomatic code; a change needs approval from someone with readability in its language. Usually one reviewer satisfies both, which is why the median reviewer count is one. The general principles transfer: make accountability explicit (CODEOWNERS on GitHub and GitLab implement ownership), and make style standards a thing that's taught and certified once rather than argued in every review.

Review as a security control, and its limits

Review is good at a specific class of security issue: logic flaws a tool can't see. Missing authorisation checks (the "insecure direct object reference" in the worked example), trusting client-supplied prices or roles, logging tokens, building SQL or shell commands from input, and in LLM applications, prompt-injection paths where retrieved documents or tool results are treated as instructions. It's weak at subtle memory-safety bugs, timing side channels and cryptographic misuse, which need specialised tooling and expert reviewers. The 2021 incident in which malicious commits were pushed to the PHP project's source repository under two maintainers' names (swe8 covers it) shows review has an adversarial dimension too: the commits were noticed and reverted by maintainers, and the project responded by retiring its self-hosted Git server and making its GitHub repositories canonical, with organisation membership and two-factor authentication required. A mature approach assigns security-owner review to sensitive paths, runs automated scanners in CI, and uses threat modelling at design time (swe13), rather than assuming generalist reviewers will catch everything.

Stacked changes and trunk-based development

Small changes only stay small if the workflow supports shipping incomplete features. Two techniques make it possible. Stacked changes let an author submit change 2 that builds on unmerged change 1, and change 3 on 2, each reviewed independently; tools such as Graphite, Sapling, git-branchless and Gerrit's relation chains manage the rebasing when an early change is revised. Feature flags let incomplete functionality merge to the main branch while switched off, so a feature can arrive in ten small changes rather than one branch that lives for weeks. Together they enable trunk-based development (swe8), in which everyone integrates into one main branch at least daily — which in turn makes every change small enough to review well. Review practice and branching strategy are two halves of the same system.

AI-assisted review, used well

LLM-based review assistants can summarise a change, flag likely bugs and suggest tests, and they're increasingly common in review tools. Used well, they handle the mechanical layer — "this except swallows everything", "this variable is unused", "this function lacks a test for the empty case" — so human reviewers can focus on design and intent. Their limits follow from how they work: they don't know the system's history, the business rules behind a design, or which of their plausible-sounding comments are false positives, and their suggestions can be confidently wrong. Treat their comments as a linter with unusually broad coverage and a high false-positive rate: helpful input to the author, never a substitute for an accountable human approval. And when the code itself was generated by a model, review matters more, not less — the author may understand it less well than code they typed, so the description should say which parts were generated and how they were verified.
prod:
How review breaks down in real teams

The failure modes are predictable. Latency spirals: reviews wait days, so authors batch work into large PRs, which take longer to review, so latency grows further. Rubber-stamping: large or unfamiliar changes get "LGTM" after a skim, especially under deadline pressure, and approvals stop meaning anything. Nit storms: dozens of style comments, often inconsistent between reviewers, that frustrate authors and bury real issues. Gatekeeping bottlenecks: one senior engineer must approve everything in an area and becomes a queue. Review as the only safety net: teams that skip tests or staged rollouts because "it was reviewed". Each is visible in data most review tools expose: time to first review, time to merge, change size distribution, rounds per change, and reviewer load per person. Watching those numbers, and discussing them in retrospectives, fixes more than exhortation does.

Case: Apple's "goto fail" (CVE-2014-1266)

In February 2014 Apple shipped an unusual security update for iOS — 7.0.6, plus 6.1.6 for older devices — with a terse note that it fixed a problem verifying secure connections, followed days later by OS X 10.9.2. The bug, published by Google engineer Adam Langley the next day, was in Apple's SecureTransport library, which implements TLS (the protocol that encrypts HTTPS connections and proves a server's identity, net9) for most software on Apple's platforms. In the function that checks the server's signature over its key-exchange parameters, the code read:

if ((err = SSLHashSHA1.update(&hashCtx, &serverRandom)) != 0)
    goto fail;
if ((err = SSLHashSHA1.update(&hashCtx, &signedParams)) != 0)
    goto fail;
    goto fail;
if ((err = SSLHashSHA1.final(&hashCtx, &hashOut)) != 0)
    goto fail;
/* ... the signature is actually verified here ... */

fail:
    SSLFreeBuffer(&signedHashes);
    SSLFreeBuffer(&hashCtx);
    return err;

The second goto fail; is indented as if it belonged to the if, but in C an if without braces governs only one statement. So after the second hash update succeeded, the duplicated line jumped unconditionally to the clean-up code, with err still 0 — success — skipping the rest of the hash computation and the actual signature check. As Langley explained, this broke the link between the server's certificate and the key used for the connection: an attacker positioned on the network (on public Wi-Fi, say) could present a genuine server's valid certificate chain but sign the handshake with a different key, or not sign it properly at all, and the client would accept it. Most software on iOS and OS X that used SecureTransport was affected; browsers such as Chrome and Firefox, which used a different TLS library, were not. The vulnerability is recorded as CVE-2014-1266.

Langley's analysis is a small lesson in defence in depth, and he was careful not to blame an individual — "I believe that it's just a mistake and I feel very bad for whoever might have slipped in an editor". He listed what could have caught it. A compiler warning: Clang had -Wunreachable-code, which flags the code after the unconditional jump, but it wasn't part of the commonly used -Wall set. Coding style: mandatory braces around if bodies make this particular slip much harder (he noted indentation can mislead with braces too). A test: a negative test that presents a handshake signed with the wrong key — hard to write because it needs a deliberately misbehaving TLS peer, which is exactly why such tests are often missing. And code review: "Code review can be effective against these sorts of bug. Not just auditing, but review of each change as it goes in." A reviewer reading the diff that introduced the duplicated line would have seen two identical goto fail; lines in a row — the kind of anomaly that a careful line-by-line read of security-critical code exists to catch. The lab's review bot catches the Python equivalent automatically.

The AI-engineering angle

LLM systems add review surfaces that many teams leave unguarded. Prompt templates edited directly in a dashboard, bypassing version control and review, are the goto-fail of AI features: a one-line change with global effect and no diff. Model version bumps in configuration change behaviour everywhere at once. Evaluation sets can be changed in the same PR as the prompt they evaluate, quietly moving the goalposts. Good practice is to treat all of these as code: prompts and model configurations in the repository, changes reviewed with evaluation results attached, evaluation-set changes reviewed separately from the prompts they grade, and rollouts behind flags (swe9). And as code generation by models becomes common, review is where a human takes responsibility for code they didn't type.

Tools and knobs

Branch protection requiring an approval and passing CI before merge; CODEOWNERS for routing and ownership; pull-request templates prompting for what, why, testing, risk and rollback; formatters, linters, type checkers and secret scanners in CI so humans never comment on style; review-latency and change-size dashboards; stacked-change tooling for large features; and a short written guide to what reviewers look for and how comments are labelled. For C and C++ codebases, treat compiler warnings like -Wunreachable-code as errors; in Python, linters flag unreachable statements, and type checkers such as mypy can report them with --warn-unreachable.
myths: The main purpose of code review is to find bugs.

Finding defects matters, but it isn't the only or even the most common outcome. Google's study of its own process found reviews serve education, maintaining norms and consistency, gatekeeping for ownership, and accident prevention, with the educational effect visible in data: newer engineers receive more than twice as many comments per change. Review is also how knowledge of a codebase spreads beyond its author, which reduces the risk of one person being the only one who understands it.
A thorough review has lots of comments.

Comment count measures the reviewer's activity, not the change's improvement. Forty comments about naming and spacing can bury the one comment that matters — a missing authorisation check — and demoralise the author. Most style issues should be caught by formatters and linters before a human looks; a good review spends attention on design, correctness, tests and risk, labels what is blocking, and may reasonably be just "LGTM" on a small, clean change.
Reviewing large changes in one go is more efficient than many small ones.

Review quality falls as change size rises: reviewers skim, useful comments per line drop, and latency grows. Google's data shows the median change is 24 lines and about 90% touch fewer than 10 files, and its review latency is correspondingly short. Small changes are also easier to roll back independently. Splitting a large feature into a stack of small, reviewable steps is faster overall, not slower.
Senior engineers' changes don't need as careful a review.

Everyone's code has bugs, and experienced engineers often work on the riskiest parts of a system. The goto-fail bug that broke TLS certificate checking on Apple's platforms was a single duplicated line that any reviewer reading the diff could have caught. Seniority changes the conversation — more design discussion, less style — not the need for a second pair of eyes.
If the tests pass, the reviewer doesn't need to look at the tests.

Passing tests only show that the tests agree with the code. A reviewer checks that the tests would fail if the behaviour were wrong: that they assert outcomes rather than just running code, cover the edge cases and error paths the change introduces, and don't depend on timing or order. A change whose new tests all pass without the new code is untested, whatever CI says.
Code review slows teams down.

Slow review slows teams down; review itself needn't. At Google the median time for the whole review process is under four hours, and most changes get at most one round of comments. The practices that make that possible — small changes, automation for style, clear descriptions, reviewers treating pending reviews as higher priority than starting new work — are the actual subject of good review culture.
lab:
Goal: build a tiny "review bot" that does what CI should do before a human looks: measure the size of a change, and flag the goto-fail shape of bug — code that can never run — plus two other review smells. Stdlib only (ast, difflib, re), Python 3.12, runs instantly.

  1. Save the script as swe6_lab.py and run python swe6_lab.py.
  2. It diffs a BEFORE and AFTER version of a small module. In AFTER, a "bad merge" left a stray return True in verify_server_key — the Python analogue of Apple's duplicated goto fail;: the signature check below it can never run, so the function accepts anything that hashes correctly. A new load_config also swallows every exception and hard-codes an API key.
  3. Expected output: the unified diff (+8 / -0 lines), then three findings:
review bot findings:
  - line 6: unreachable after 'return True'
  - line 13: broad exception swallowed (except ...: pass)
  - line 15: possible hard-coded secret

What it shows. The unreachable-code check walks every block in the syntax tree and reports any statement that follows a return, raise, continue or break in the same block. It needs no understanding of cryptography to find a critical bug — which is exactly why such checks belong in CI, freeing human reviewers for the questions only they can answer, like "does this endpoint check the caller owns the invoice?"

Try next: (1) Delete the stray line from AFTER; the unreachable finding disappears and the assertion len(findings) == 3 fails, telling you to update it. (2) Add a rule that flags a changed source file with no corresponding test file changed. (3) Run the real tools on your own code: ruff check --select B,BLE,E722,S105 and mypy --warn-unreachable.

"""swe6 lab: a tiny review bot — size a change, then flag unreachable code (the 'goto fail' shape) and other review smells."""
import ast
import difflib
import re

BEFORE = '''
def verify_server_key(msg, sig, key):
    if not hash_ok(msg):
        return False
    if not check_signature(msg, sig, key):
        return False
    return True
'''

AFTER = '''
def verify_server_key(msg, sig, key):
    if not hash_ok(msg):
        return False
    return True                      # left behind by a bad merge
    if not check_signature(msg, sig, key):
        return False
    return True

def load_config(path):
    try:
        return json.load(open(path))
    except Exception:
        pass
    api_key = "sk-live-4f9c2d0e8b7a61"
'''

def diff_stats(before: str, after: str) -> tuple[int, int, list[str]]:
    diff = list(difflib.unified_diff(before.splitlines(), after.splitlines(), "before.py", "after.py", lineterm="", n=1))
    added = sum(1 for l in diff if l.startswith("+") and not l.startswith("+++"))
    removed = sum(1 for l in diff if l.startswith("-") and not l.startswith("---"))
    return added, removed, diff

def unreachable(tree: ast.AST) -> list[str]:
    """Statements that follow return/raise/continue/break in the same block can never run."""
    found = []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        for field in ("body", "orelse", "finalbody", "handlers"):
            block = getattr(node, field, None)
            if not isinstance(block, list):
                continue
            for stmt, nxt in zip(block, block[1:]):
                if isinstance(stmt, (ast.Return, ast.Raise, ast.Continue, ast.Break)):
                    found.append(f"line {nxt.lineno}: unreachable after '{ast.unparse(stmt)}'")
    return found

def smells(tree: ast.AST, src: str) -> list[str]:
    out = []
    for node in ast.walk(tree):
        if isinstance(node, ast.ExceptHandler):
            broad = node.type is None or (isinstance(node.type, ast.Name) and node.type.id in {"Exception", "BaseException"})
            if broad and all(isinstance(s, ast.Pass) for s in node.body):
                out.append(f"line {node.lineno}: broad exception swallowed (except ...: pass)")
    for i, line in enumerate(src.splitlines(), 1):
        if re.search(r"""(api_key|secret|password|token)\s*=\s*["'][^"']{8,}["']""", line, re.I):
            out.append(f"line {i}: possible hard-coded secret")
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    added, removed, diff = diff_stats(BEFORE, AFTER)
    print(f"change size: +{added} / -{removed} lines")
    print("\n".join(diff))
    tree = ast.parse(AFTER)
    findings = unreachable(tree) + smells(tree, AFTER)
    print("\nreview bot findings:")
    for f in findings:
        print("  -", f)
    assert any("unreachable" in f for f in findings)
    assert len(findings) == 3
recap: Code review catches defects, but just as importantly spreads knowledge, keeps the codebase consistent, and ensures owners of each area see changes to it.
The author's job is to make review easy: a small change with one purpose, a description that says what, why, how it was tested and how to roll it back, and a self-review before asking anyone else.
Google's data on 9 million reviewed changes: median change of 24 lines, about 90% touching fewer than 10 files, a median of one reviewer, and a median review time under four hours.

Reviewers look in order of importance: does the change solve the right problem with a sound design, is it correct including edge cases and concurrency, do the tests prove it, is it secure and operable, and only then is it readable.
Automate everything a machine can check — formatting, lint, types, secret scanning — so human attention goes where only humans can help.
Feedback lands when it explains why, labels severity (blocking, suggestion, nit), asks rather than commands, and addresses the code, not the person; after two rounds of disagreement, talk.
Review latency is a team metric: aim to respond within hours and treat reviews as higher priority than starting new work.

Apple's 2014 goto-fail bug — a duplicated line that made signature verification always succeed — is the canonical example of a one-line defect that review of the diff, a compiler warning or a negative test would have caught.
Changes to configuration, migrations, dependencies, prompts and model versions deserve review as rigorous as code, with evidence attached such as a migration plan or evaluation results.
glossary: Blocking comment
A review comment that must be resolved before the change can merge, as opposed to a suggestion or nit.
CI (continuous integration)
The system that builds and tests every change automatically before and after it merges.
CODEOWNERS
A file in a repository mapping paths to the people or teams whose approval is required for changes there.
Conventional comments
A lightweight convention of prefixing review comments with a label such as issue, suggestion, question, nit or praise, plus whether it is blocking.
CVE
Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures: the public catalogue that gives each known security vulnerability an ID such as CVE-2014-1266.
Dead code
Code that can never run, or whose result is never used; in a diff it often signals a merge error or a mistake.
Expand–contract
Changing a shared schema or interface in backward-compatible steps: add the new form, migrate users, then remove the old form (swe9 covers it).
LGTM
"Looks good to me": the conventional approval in a code review.
LLM (large language model)
A neural network that generates text from a prompt; prompts and model versions that configure it change behaviour and deserve review like code.
Nit
A minor, non-blocking comment about style or preference, which the author may take or leave.
Pair programming
Two engineers working on the same code at the same time, one typing and one reviewing continuously.
Pull request (PR)
A proposed change to a repository, with its diff, description and discussion, submitted for review before merging; also called a merge request or changelist (CL).
Readability (Google)
Google's certification that an engineer writes idiomatic code in a given language; changes need approval from someone with readability.
Review latency
The time from a change being sent for review to receiving feedback or approval.
Rubber-stamping
Approving a change without genuinely reviewing it.
Self-review
The author reading their own diff as a reviewer would before requesting review.
Stacked changes
A sequence of small dependent changes, each reviewed and merged separately, that together deliver a larger feature.
Static analysis
Automated checking of code without running it — linters, type checkers, security scanners.
TLS
Transport Layer Security, the protocol that encrypts connections and proves a server's identity with certificates and signatures (net9).
Unreachable code
Statements that can never execute because every path to them returns, raises or jumps away first.
drill:
Handle it

A teammate's 1,400-line PR adds a new payments endpoint. It includes a refactor of the shared HTTP client, a schema migration, the endpoint, and tests. You spot that the migration drops a column the old service version still reads. How do you respond?

Answer

Blocking issue first, clearly labelled: dropping a column that the currently deployed version reads will break production during the rollout, when old and new versions run side by side. Propose expand–contract (swe9): this PR stops reading and writing the column; a later PR drops it after the old version is gone. Link to the team's migration guidelines if you have them.

Structure: ask to split into (1) the HTTP client refactor with no behaviour change, (2) the migration, (3) the endpoint behind a flag. Explain it's about review quality and safe rollback — each piece can be reverted independently — not about style. Offer to help split it or to pair on it if it's urgent.

Then the normal review on the endpoint, in priority order: authorisation (can one customer act on another's payment?), idempotency-key handling for payment retries, timeouts on the provider call, error handling that doesn't turn provider outages into "declined", and logging without card data.

Tone: a short summary comment or a call rather than 40 line comments; acknowledge the work and anything done well. This is the answer shape interviewers want: protect production, improve the process, keep the relationship.
qa: E
What is code review for?

To catch defects and design problems before they ship, but also to spread knowledge of the codebase beyond each author, keep code consistent with team norms, let owners of an area see changes to it, and teach — newer engineers learn conventions and the system through review comments. A process that only hunts bugs misses most of its value.
E
What makes a pull request easy to review?

It's small and has one purpose; its description says what changed, why, how it was tested and how to roll it back; it separates pure refactors from behaviour changes; generated files and formatting churn are kept out or clearly marked; and the author has self-reviewed it and left comments on anything non-obvious. Tests are included and demonstrate the behaviour.
E
What do you do when you disagree with a reviewer?

Assume good intent and look for the underlying concern. Explain my reasoning with evidence — a benchmark, a link, a test — rather than repeating the position. If we still disagree after a couple of rounds, move to a call; if it's a matter of taste with no team standard, defer to whoever owns the code or record a decision so it isn't relitigated; if it matters, escalate to a tech lead with both options written down.
M
What do you look for when reviewing, and in what order?

First, is this the right change — does it solve the stated problem, is the design sound, does it belong here? Second, correctness: edge cases, error paths, concurrency, data migrations, backward compatibility. Third, tests: would they fail if the behaviour broke? Fourth, security, performance and operability — authorisation, input validation, logging, metrics, rollout. Last, readability and naming. Style is left to tools.
Follow-up: how long should a review take? — Most small changes take minutes to half an hour; if a change needs more than about an hour of focused reading, it is usually too big and should be split.
M
How do you give critical feedback that the author will act on?

Comment on the code, not the person; explain why, not just what ('this read-then-write can race under concurrent requests'); suggest a concrete alternative; label severity so blocking issues stand out from nits; ask questions when unsure rather than asserting; and note what's good. If there are many issues of one kind, say so once rather than forty times, and offer to pair.
M
How do you keep review latency low across a team?

Keep changes small, automate style and simple checks, write good descriptions, and set a norm that reviews are answered within a few hours and take priority over starting new work. Route reviews with CODEOWNERS or round-robin so no one person is a bottleneck, track time-to-first-review as a team metric, and allow merging after approval with non-blocking comments addressed in follow-ups.
M
What should automation handle so humans don't have to?

Formatting (Black, Ruff format), lint rules (Ruff), type checking (mypy, pyright), tests and coverage reports, dependency and licence checks, secret scanning, and known-vulnerability scanning. Automated review comments on unreachable code, broad exception handlers and complexity thresholds help too. Anything a tool can decide consistently shouldn't consume human review time or cause arguments.
M
How would you review a change to an LLM prompt or model configuration?

Treat it like code with behaviour. The diff should be readable — prompt templates in version-controlled files, not strings buried in code — and the description should include evaluation results on the standard set compared with the current version, with examples of changed outputs. Check for regressions on important slices, cost and latency changes, and that the change is behind a flag or versioned so it can be rolled back.
Follow-up: what if there's no evaluation set? — Then the first request is to create a small one from real examples before approving; otherwise nobody can tell whether the change helped.
M
Explain the goto-fail bug and what would have caught it.

In 2014 Apple's TLS code had a duplicated 'goto fail;' after an if statement. The first was conditional; the second, despite its indentation, always ran, jumping to the clean-up label with err still set to success, so the final signature check in the server key exchange was skipped and any signature was accepted. Review of the diff, a compiler warning for unreachable code, mandatory braces, or a negative test that presents a bad signature would each have caught it.
H
A teammate's 1,400-line PR mixes a refactor, a schema migration and a new endpoint. How do you handle it?

Lead with any blocking correctness issue — for example a migration that drops a column the currently deployed version still reads. Then ask to split it into a behaviour-preserving refactor, the migration done expand–contract, and the endpoint, explaining it's about review quality and independent rollback rather than style. Offer to help split it. Then review the endpoint for authorisation, idempotency, timeouts and logging. Deliver it as a short summary or a call rather than dozens of comments.
H
How do you decide how many reviewers a change needs?

By risk and ownership, not by habit. Most changes need one reviewer who knows the area, which Google's data shows works at scale. Add a second for changes crossing ownership boundaries, security-sensitive code (authentication, cryptography, payments), irreversible operations (data migrations, deletions), and infrastructure affecting many services. More reviewers than needed diffuses responsibility and slows everything, since each assumes another looked closely.

Follow-up: how do you prevent rubber-stamping? — Keep changes small enough to read, rotate reviewers, make it acceptable to say 'I'm not the right reviewer for this part', and sample-audit approvals in retrospectives.
H
How do you raise code review quality across an organisation?

Write down what reviewers should look for and the comment conventions, so expectations are shared. Automate style and simple checks. Measure time to first review, rounds per change and change size, not comment counts. Teach through review — pair senior and junior reviewers on complex changes. Use escaped defects: when a bug reaches production, ask whether review could have caught it and what would have helped, blamelessly. And make it normal to review design before code for large changes.
H
What's the role of code review in security?

Review is one layer, good at catching logic flaws tools miss: missing authorisation checks, trusting client input, secrets in code, unsafe deserialisation, prompt-injection paths in LLM features where retrieved text can issue instructions. It's weak at subtle memory-safety or cryptographic issues, which need specialised tools and expert review. So require security-owner review for sensitive paths, run automated scanners in CI, and use threat modelling at design time (swe13) rather than hoping review finds everything.

A labelling scheme that makes the intent and severity of review comments explicit.
What to look for in a code review
Google's reviewer checklist: design, functionality, complexity, tests, naming, comments, style, documentation.

t: API design: REST, gRPC and GraphQL
sum: Designing interfaces other teams build on: resources and methods, status codes and error contracts, idempotency keys, cursor pagination, long-running operations, versioning without breaking anyone (Stripe's date-based model), and REST vs gRPC vs GraphQL traced byte by byte for the same call — plus what changes for LLM APIs.
prereq: net7
HTTP semantics: methods (GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE), which are safe and idempotent, status-code classes, and headers such as Content-Type and Retry-After.
net8
HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection with binary framing; HTTP/3 does the same over QUIC.
swe4
Failures come in kinds — bugs, expected outcomes, transient faults — and callers need to tell them apart; retries are safe only for idempotent operations.
swe1
An interface is a contract; callers depend on everything observable about it, so narrow, stable interfaces keep change local.
why:
A mobile banking app sends "transfer £25" over a train's patchy connection. The request reaches the server and the transfer happens, but the response is lost in a tunnel. The app, seeing a timeout, retries. The customer is charged twice. The same month, the platform team renames a response field from verified to status because the new name is clearer; three partner integrations break overnight, because their code checked verified. And a support dashboard that pages through transactions with ?offset=20 shows some transactions twice and silently skips others whenever new ones arrive while an agent is scrolling.

None of these is a bug in the usual sense. Each is an API design decision — or a missing one. An API (application programming interface) is the contract through which other code talks to yours: which operations exist, what they accept, what they return, how they fail, and how all of that may change over time. Internal code can be refactored freely because you can update every caller in one change; an API's callers are in other teams, other companies, and apps installed on phones you'll never update. Once one client depends on a behaviour, changing it has a cost you don't control. That makes API design one of the few areas of software where getting it right up front really matters.

This lesson covers the design decisions that come up in every API and every interview about one: modelling resources and methods; status codes and machine-readable errors; idempotency keys that make retries safe; cursor pagination that doesn't skip or duplicate; long-running operations; and versioning and compatibility, using Stripe's published approach as the case study — a company that has kept every version of its API working since 2011. Then the three main styles, REST, gRPC and GraphQL, compared on the same call, down to the bytes on the wire. Finally, what's different about APIs that serve or call large language models (LLMs): streaming, pinned model versions, tool schemas and agents that retry. The lab encodes one response both ways by hand and simulates pagination and retries.
primer:
The analogy: a restaurant's menu and ordering system

A restaurant's menu is its API. It lists what you can order (operations), what you must specify (parameters: size, how cooked), and what you'll get back. The kitchen can change freely behind the pass — new ovens, new staff, a new supplier — as long as the dish that arrives matches the menu. But change the menu carelessly and regulars are upset: remove a dish, and people who came for it leave; quietly change what "large" means, and everyone who ordered large feels cheated. Good restaurants add new dishes freely, announce removals well in advance, and never change what an existing item means. And a good ordering system is safe to repeat: if a waiter isn't sure the kitchen got an order, they can check the ticket number rather than placing the order again and serving two meals.

The analogy breaks on scale and memory. A restaurant's regulars can be told about changes; an API may have thousands of clients whose authors have moved on, running code nobody will touch for years. They can't adapt, so the API must.

Three styles for the same call

Suppose a client wants invoice 48213. The three dominant API styles express that call differently:

Whichever style you choose, the same questions come up: what are the nouns and operations? How do failures look, so a client knows whether to fix, retry or give up? What happens when a request is sent twice? How does a client walk through a million records? And how will this contract change over the next five years without breaking anyone? Those questions, not the choice of style, decide whether an API is good. Get them right and switching the transport later is a manageable project; get them wrong and no transport will save you, because every client has already written code against the mistakes.

It also helps to know who the client is, because that shapes almost every choice. A public API used by other companies must be conservative: universal tooling, generous compatibility, careful deprecation, documentation good enough that nobody needs to ask you. A partner or mobile API has fewer clients, but ones you can't force to upgrade — apps stay installed for years. An internal service-to-service API has clients you can find and update, so it can use stricter contracts and more efficient transports, and breaking changes can be coordinated, though they still need care. The same endpoint design can be excellent for one audience and wrong for another; a senior answer to any API design question starts by asking who will call it and how hard they are to change.

One principle underlies all of them: design from the client's use cases, not from your database. An API that mirrors your tables leaks your internal structure into every client, so any schema change becomes an API change. An API designed around what clients need to do — "list a customer's unpaid invoices", "pay this invoice" — lets the implementation change behind it, exactly the information hiding from swe1.
body:
1. Resources, identifiers and methods

Resource-oriented design, the backbone of REST and of Google's API guidelines, starts by naming the resources — the nouns — and arranging them in a hierarchy that reflects ownership: /customers/{customer_id}/invoices/{invoice_id}. Collections are plural nouns; individual resources are addressed by ID. Operations then use a small set of standard methods with the semantics HTTP already defines (net7): GET to read, POST to a collection to create, PUT to replace, PATCH to partially update, DELETE to remove. A client that knows the pattern for one resource knows it for all.

Identifiers should be opaque, stable strings, not database row numbers the client might do arithmetic on. Stripe's IDs carry a type prefix (cus_, ch_, in_), so a customer ID pasted into an invoice field fails fast with a clear message, and logs are readable. Sequential integer IDs also leak information (how many invoices you have) and invite enumeration attacks, where an attacker increments the ID to read other customers' data — so every read must check the caller owns the resource (swe13).

Some operations don't fit create-read-update-delete: send an invoice, cancel a job, refund a payment. Model them as custom methods on the resource — POST /invoices/{id}:send in Google's style, or POST /invoices/{id}/send — rather than contorting them into a PATCH of a status field, which hides the side effects (an email is sent) behind what looks like a data update. A related trick: when an action creates something with its own lifecycle, make that a resource — a refund is POST /refunds with a charge field, and the refund then has its own ID and status.

Two design details prevent whole classes of bugs. Money is an integer in minor units with a currency — {"amount": 129900, "currency": "EUR"} means €1,299.00 — because floating-point numbers can't represent most decimal fractions exactly (swe1, swe4). Timestamps are ISO 8601 in UTC with an explicit offset (2026-09-29T14:03:00Z). Names carry units wherever a number has them (timeout_ms, size_bytes).

2. Status codes and an error contract

A status code's main job is to tell the client — and every proxy, load balancer and library between them — what kind of outcome this is and therefore what to do next:

StatusMeaningClient should…
200 / 201 / 204Success / created / no bodyproceed
202Accepted, not finishedpoll the status resource
400Malformed requestfix the request; don't retry
401 / 403Not authenticated / not allowedre-authenticate / stop
404No such resource (or not yours)stop
409Conflicts with current statere-read, then decide
422Valid shape, fails a business ruleshow the user; don't retry
429Rate limitedwait Retry-After, then retry
500Server bugreport; maybe retry once
503Temporarily unavailableretry with backoff

This is swe4's failure triage expressed on the wire: 4xx says "your request is the problem, retrying won't help", 429 and 503 say "transient, retry later", 500 says "our bug". Returning 200 with {"error": ...} in the body, or 500 for a validation failure, breaks every generic client and retry library that relies on the status class. Note the 404-for-403 choice: if revealing that invoice 48213 exists would leak information to a caller who can't see it, respond as if it doesn't.

The body needs a machine-readable contract too. RFC 9457 "problem details" standardises it as application/problem+json:

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Content
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.example.com/errors/insufficient-funds",
  "title": "Insufficient funds",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Account acc_1 has 1,200 EUR; the transfer needs 2,500 EUR.",
  "instance": "/v1/transfers/tr_123",
  "code": "insufficient_funds",
  "request_id": "req_7Hc2"
}

Clients branch on type or a stable code, never on the human-readable detail, which you should be free to reword. For validation errors, list every invalid field at once rather than failing on the first. Include a request ID so support can find the logs, and never include stack traces or internal hostnames.

3. Idempotency: making retries safe

Recall the doubled transfer. The client can't distinguish "the request never arrived" from "it arrived, succeeded, and the response was lost"; both look like a timeout. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent — repeating them has the same effect as doing them once — so retrying is safe. POST isn't. The standard fix is the idempotency key: the client generates a unique value (a random UUID) once per logical operation — per tap of the "Send" button, not per HTTP attempt — and sends it with the request and every retry.

POST /v1/transfers
Idempotency-Key: 5f0c7a8e-2b41-4d0e-9c7e-1b2f3a4d5e6f
{"from": "acc_1", "to": "acc_9", "amount": 2500, "currency": "GBP"}

Trace the server's side. First attempt: the key is new. In one database transaction the server creates the transfer and stores (key, hash(request body), response). It sends 201, which is lost. Retry with the same key: the server finds the key, checks the body hash matches, and returns the stored 201 response without creating anything. The client now has its answer and exactly one transfer exists. Three edge cases need rules. Same key, different body: almost certainly a client bug — reject it (Stripe compares parameters and errors if they differ). A retry arriving while the first attempt is still running: return 409 and let the client retry later, rather than running both. Retention: keys can't be kept forever; Stripe's documentation says keys may be pruned after they're at least 24 hours old, after which reuse creates a new request. Stripe stores the first response for a key whether it succeeded or failed — including 500 errors — but not failures that happen before execution begins, such as validation errors, which can simply be retried. The key must be stored in the same transaction as the side effect; otherwise a crash between the two leaves a transfer without a key, and the retry duplicates it.

4. Pagination: offset versus cursor

No list endpoint should return unbounded results. Offset pagination (?offset=40&limit=20) is easy to implement and allows jumping to page 7, but has two problems. It's slow for deep pages, because the database must find and discard every skipped row. And it's unstable when data changes between requests. The lab traces it. Ten orders are listed newest first, four per page. The client fetches page 1 (orders 1–4). Two new orders arrive, which go to the top. The client fetches page 2 with offset=4 — but the first four rows are now the two new orders plus orders 1 and 2, so rows 5–8 are orders 3, 4, 5 and 6. Orders 3 and 4 appear twice. Had two orders been deleted instead, two unseen orders would have been skipped silently.

Cursor pagination (also called keyset pagination) fixes both problems. The response includes an opaque next_cursor that encodes the sort key of the last item — for "newest first", its (created_at, id), with the ID as a tie-breaker — and the next query asks for rows after that key: WHERE (created_at, id) < (:ts, :id) ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20. With an index on (created_at, id), every page is equally fast, and inserts or deletes elsewhere don't shift it. The cursor should be opaque to clients (base64-encoded, perhaps signed) so you can change its contents later. The trade-offs: no jumping to page 7, and exact total counts, which require scanning everything, should be optional or approximate.

5. Long-running operations

Some operations take longer than a client can sensibly hold a request open: fine-tuning a model, generating a large report, a bank transfer that settles in a minute. Holding the HTTP request open for minutes ties up connections, fails on every proxy timeout, and loses the result if the client disconnects. The pattern is to return 202 Accepted immediately with a resource representing the job:

POST /v1/reports   (Idempotency-Key: ...)
202 Accepted
Location: /v1/reports/rep_42
{"id": "rep_42", "status": "queued"}

GET /v1/reports/rep_42   →  {"status": "running", "progress": 0.6}
GET /v1/reports/rep_42   →  {"status": "succeeded", "result_url": "..."}

The job has explicit states (queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled — a state machine, swe3), and clients either poll with backoff or register a webhook: a URL the provider calls when the job changes state. Webhooks need their own care: sign them so receivers can verify the sender, retry until acknowledged, include an event ID so receivers can deduplicate, and provide an events endpoint so a receiver that was down can catch up. Streaming (below) suits results produced incrementally, but the job itself should survive a disconnected client.

6. Versioning and compatibility

Every change to an API is either backward compatible — existing clients keep working — or breaking. Compatible, for well-behaved clients: adding an endpoint, adding an optional request parameter, adding a response field, relaxing a validation. Breaking: removing or renaming a field, changing its type or format (an integer ID becoming a string), changing a default, making an optional parameter required, tightening validation, changing an error's status code, and — the sneakiest — changing what a field means while keeping its shape. Enum values sit in between: adding "disputed" to a status field is compatible only if clients were told to handle unknown values.

Clients help by being tolerant readers: ignore fields you don't recognise, handle unknown enum values with a default branch, and don't depend on field order. Providers help by documenting that they will add fields and values, and by testing compatibility automatically — diffing the OpenAPI or protobuf schema in CI with a breaking-change detector.

When a breaking change is truly needed, a versioning scheme decides how it's delivered. The common one is a major version in the URL (/v1/, /v2/) or a header. Its weakness, as Stripe's engineers put it, is that changes between major versions are so big that upgrading is almost as painful as integrating from scratch, so many clients never upgrade and the provider maintains old versions indefinitely. The case study below describes Stripe's alternative: many small, date-named versions. Whatever the scheme, deprecation needs process: announce the change, give a timeline, measure who still uses the old behaviour (per-client usage metrics), contact them, and signal it in responses (the Deprecation and Sunset HTTP headers exist for this).

One law makes all of this harder than the contract suggests. Hyrum's law, named after Google engineer Hyrum Wright: "With a sufficient number of users of an API, it does not matter what you promise in the contract: all observable behaviors of your system will be depended on by somebody." The order of results you never promised, the wording of an error message, a response that happened to arrive in 50 ms — somebody depends on it. Defences: make the contract explicit (stable error codes, not messages), avoid accidental observable behaviour (sort results deliberately or randomise what isn't promised), and roll out even "compatible" changes gradually, watching error rates by client.

7. REST, gRPC and GraphQL compared on the wire

REST over JSON is the default for public APIs. It works from any language and any browser, debugs with curl, and uses HTTP caching (Cache-Control, ETag) and every proxy and gateway built for it. Its weaknesses are a loose contract unless you add a schema (OpenAPI), verbose payloads, and fixed response shapes that over-fetch (fields the client doesn't need) or under-fetch (requiring extra round trips).

gRPC defines services and messages in Protocol Buffers and generates client and server code in many languages. Calls travel over HTTP/2 (net8), which multiplexes many calls on one connection and supports streaming in both directions. To see where its efficiency comes from, encode the invoice from the primer. As compact JSON — {"id":48213,"customer_id":"cus_9f2k","amount_cents":129900,"currency":"EUR","status":"PAID"} — it is 92 bytes. The protobuf schema numbers each field:

message Invoice {
  int64  id           = 1;
  string customer_id  = 2;
  int64  amount_cents = 3;
  string currency     = 4;
  Status status       = 5;   // enum Status { DRAFT = 0; OPEN = 1; PAID = 2; }
}

On the wire, each field is a tag — the field number shifted left three bits, OR'd with a 3-bit wire type (0 for varint integers, 2 for length-delimited strings and bytes) — followed by the value. Integers use varints: seven bits per byte, least-significant group first, with the top bit set on every byte except the last.

The encoding is about a quarter of the size, and parsing binary integers is cheaper than parsing decimal text. That matters for high-volume internal traffic; for most APIs, database time dominates and compressed JSON narrows the gap. gRPC's bigger wins are the typed contract (a .proto file is the single source of truth, and breaking changes can be detected mechanically), generated clients, streaming, and deadlines: a client says "I need an answer within 300 ms", and the deadline propagates through every downstream call, so servers stop working on requests nobody is waiting for. Its costs: browsers can't call gRPC directly (gRPC-Web and a proxy are needed), binary traffic is harder to inspect, and HTTP caching doesn't apply. Protobuf's evolution rules follow from the encoding: never reuse or renumber a field (mark removed ones reserved), new fields are optional and old readers skip unknown ones, and renaming a field is safe on the wire but not in JSON mappings or generated code.

GraphQL exposes a typed schema through a single endpoint, and the client sends a query naming exactly the fields and related objects it wants. A mobile screen that needs an invoice's amount and its customer's email gets both in one round trip and nothing else. That flexibility moves work to the server: each field has a resolver, and a naive query for 100 invoices with their customers runs 1 + 100 database queries — the N+1 problem — unless resolvers batch (the DataLoader pattern). Public GraphQL APIs need query depth and cost limits, since a client can write an arbitrarily expensive query, and HTTP caching is harder because everything is a POST to one URL. GraphQL typically evolves without versions: add fields freely, mark old ones @deprecated, and remove them once usage tracking shows no one queries them.
