8. APIs for and around LLMs

Model-serving APIs follow every principle above, with a few twists worth knowing. Streaming: generating a long answer takes seconds, so responses are streamed token by token, most often as server-sent events (a long-lived HTTP response carrying a sequence of data: lines), with a final event carrying token usage and a stop reason. Pinned model versions: model behaviour changes between releases, so providers publish dated snapshots and deprecation schedules, and serious clients pin a specific version and upgrade deliberately after evaluation — the same logic as Stripe's pinned API versions. Schemas as contracts: tool (function) definitions and structured-output formats are JSON Schemas, and changing a tool's parameters is an API change for the model that calls it; version them. Rate limits in tokens as well as requests, returned with 429 and headers saying when capacity resets. And idempotency for agents: when a model-driven agent calls your API to take an action — issue a refund, send an email — it may retry after a timeout just like a flaky mobile client, so actions with side effects need idempotency keys, and dangerous ones a confirmation step.
deep:
Designing from use cases: the API review

The cheapest time to fix an API is before its first client. Mature organisations run a lightweight API design review: a short document with the resources, methods, request and response examples, error cases and pagination, reviewed by people who've designed many APIs, against written guidelines (Google's AIPs, Microsoft's REST guidelines or an internal equivalent). Stripe describes exactly this: outgoing changes are written up in a brief document and sent to an internal mailing list, so errors and inconsistencies are caught before they ship. The review's questions are mostly about consistency and future change. Does this look like our other APIs? Are the nouns right — would a second use case fit without a new endpoint? Which fields might need to become lists later (a single email that should have been emails is a breaking change to fix)? Which booleans should be enums (is_paid can't grow a "partially refunded" state; status can)? What happens at 10× the data?

Consistency beats local elegance

An API surface with 200 endpoints designed by 30 people is only usable if it's consistent: the same pagination parameters everywhere, the same error shape, the same naming conventions (snake_case or camelCase, never both), the same way of expanding related objects, the same timestamp format. Each inconsistency is a small tax on every client developer, forever. That's why large API programmes enforce style mechanically — OpenAPI linters such as Spectral, Google's api-linter for protobuf — and why a slightly awkward convention applied everywhere beats a locally nicer one used in one place.

Authorisation is part of the API design

The most common serious API vulnerability, top of the OWASP API Security list, is broken object-level authorisation: an endpoint that checks the caller is logged in but not that the object they asked for is theirs — the GET /invoices/{id} from swe6. Resource-oriented APIs make it easy to miss because every endpoint takes IDs. Defences are structural: scope every query by the caller's tenant (WHERE customer_id = :caller) in a shared data-access layer rather than in each handler; use unguessable IDs as defence in depth (never as the only defence); return 404 rather than 403 for objects the caller can't see; and add tests that call every endpoint with another tenant's IDs. Related design points: rate limits per client and per operation, and field-level controls so a response model never serialises internal fields by accident (swe13 covers these).

Retries, deadlines and backpressure across API boundaries

API design decides how failures propagate. A 503 with Retry-After: 30 lets well-behaved clients back off together; a 500 without guidance invites immediate retries that amplify an overload. gRPC deadlines make timeouts part of every call's contract: a caller's remaining budget shrinks as the call passes through services, and a service receiving a request with 5 ms left should fail fast instead of starting a 200 ms query. Clients should use exponential backoff with jitter, cap retries, and respect Retry-After; servers should shed load early with 429 or 503 rather than queueing work that will time out anyway (sc12 covers these resilience patterns). For LLM providers, where capacity is expensive and bursty, these signals — 429s with reset times, per-model quotas — are a large part of the practical API.

Schema evolution in practice: protobuf, JSON and events

The same compatibility logic applies to every schema that crosses a boundary: API payloads, messages on queues, and events. Two directions matter. Backward compatibility means new code can read old data (a new consumer reading last month's events). Forward compatibility means old code can read new data (an un-upgraded consumer reading events from a newer producer), which is why tolerant readers matter. Protobuf gives both if you follow its rules: new fields get new numbers, removed fields are reserved, and readers ignore unknown fields. JSON gives both only by convention. Schema registries for event streams (for example with Avro or protobuf on Kafka) enforce a chosen compatibility mode on every new schema version, rejecting breaking changes at publish time — the event-stream equivalent of a breaking-change check in CI.

REST's original constraints, and why hypermedia rarely caught on

Fielding's REST includes a constraint most "REST APIs" skip: hypermedia as the engine of application state (HATEOAS) — responses contain links to the actions available next, so clients discover the API by following links rather than hard-coding URLs, as a browser does with a website. In principle this lets servers change URLs and workflows without breaking clients. In practice, API clients are programs written against documentation, not users exploring, so few APIs go beyond including a next link for pagination and Location headers for created resources. It's worth knowing the term for interviews, and knowing that the parts of REST that deliver most value in practice are stateless requests, correct method semantics, cacheability and stable resource identifiers.
prod:
How API problems show up in production

API failures are rarely dramatic outages; they're slow leaks of trust and cost. Duplicate side effects from retries without idempotency: double charges, duplicate orders, emails sent twice — visible as support tickets and refund volume. Accidental breaking changes: a serialiser upgrade that changes date formats, a new validation rule, a field that becomes nullable — visible as a spike in 4xx errors from particular clients right after a deploy, if you break errors down by client ID and API version. Pagination anomalies in exports and syncs. Retry storms after an outage, when every client retries at once with no backoff. Deep-offset queries that slow the database as datasets grow. The observability that catches them: request metrics by endpoint, status class, client and API version; logs with request and idempotency IDs; alerts on 4xx rate changes per client after deploys; and a breaking-change check in CI on every schema diff.

Case: Stripe's API versioning

Stripe provides payment infrastructure that many businesses call directly from their own code, which makes it an unusually strict test of API evolution: a breaking change can stop other companies taking money. In a 2017 post, engineer Brandur Leach described how Stripe handles it. The starting point is a firm commitment: "we've maintained compatibility with every version of our API since the company's inception in 2011." The post gives a concrete example of the kind of change that would break clients: in 2014 Stripe replaced a bank account's boolean verified field with a status field that might contain the value "verified". Code that checked bank_account[:verified] would break, so the change was delivered as a new version rather than imposed on everyone.

The scheme has three parts. First, date-named rolling versions (for example 2017-05-24) instead of big v1/v2 releases: each contains a small set of breaking changes, so upgrading one version at a time is easy. Second, pinning: the first time an account makes an API request, it's pinned to the latest version, and every later request gets that version implicitly, so no one receives a breaking change by accident; any single request can override it with a Stripe-Version header, and accounts upgrade deliberately. Third, version-change modules: every response is described by an "API resource" class written for the current version; each breaking change is encapsulated in a module with a description, a transformation and the resource types it affects, and the modules are listed by version. To answer a request, the API renders the response at the current version and walks backwards through the list, applying each transformation until it reaches the target version — taken from the Stripe-Version header if present, then an OAuth application's version, then the account's pinned version. Old versions therefore live at the edge, not in business logic.

The post is candid about costs. Changes with side effects beyond reshaping a response (such as a different transfers behaviour) can't be encapsulated and leave checks scattered through the code, so Stripe avoids them. Every version adds code to maintain. So Stripe tries hard not to need versioning at all, through the design review described in the deep section, and the modules double as data: the public changelog and per-user documentation annotations are generated from them. The result, by the time of the post: almost a hundred backwards-incompatible upgrades over six years without breaking a single pinned integration. The same idea — pin to a dated version, upgrade deliberately, transform at the edge — is now how LLM providers publish models, and how teams should consume them.

AI systems: the API is also a model

For AI engineers, API design shows up in two directions. Serving: a model endpoint needs versioned model identifiers, streaming, clear errors for context-length overflow (a 400 with a machine-readable code, not a 500), token-based quotas, and idempotency for any endpoint that triggers side effects. Consuming: pin model versions and treat a version bump like a dependency upgrade that goes through evaluation (swe5); wrap provider SDKs in an adapter (swe2) that translates rate-limit and overload errors into your own retryable types; respect Retry-After; and when you expose tools to an agent, design them as carefully as a public API — narrow operations, explicit schemas, idempotency keys and confirmation for anything irreversible — because the model is a client that will send unexpected inputs and retry without being asked.
myths: REST means using JSON over HTTP with nice URLs.

REST, from Roy Fielding's 2000 dissertation, is an architectural style whose constraints include statelessness, cacheability and a uniform interface in which clients manipulate resources through representations. Most "REST APIs" in practice are resource-oriented HTTP APIs that follow some of those constraints, which is fine — but the useful parts to get right are the ones that affect clients: correct method semantics, meaningful status codes, cacheability, and stable resource identifiers, not the URL aesthetics.
Adding a field or an enum value is always a backward-compatible change.

Adding an optional response field is safe for clients that ignore unknown fields — but not for clients that validate responses strictly, or for generated code in some languages. Adding an enum value is riskier: a client with a switch statement over the known values may crash or mis-handle the new one. APIs should document that unknown fields and enum values must be tolerated, and treat enum additions as changes that need announcement.
gRPC is always faster than REST.

gRPC's binary Protocol Buffers encoding is smaller and cheaper to parse than JSON — the lab's invoice is 25 bytes versus 92 — and HTTP/2 multiplexing avoids per-request connection costs. But for most APIs the time goes into database queries and business logic, not encoding, and compressed JSON over HTTP/2 closes much of the gap. gRPC's bigger advantages are the typed contract, generated clients, streaming and deadline propagation; its costs are poorer browser support, harder debugging and caching.
GraphQL removes the need for API versioning and solves over-fetching for free.

GraphQL lets clients select exactly the fields they need, which removes over-fetching and lets fields be added without new endpoints. But removing or changing a field still breaks the clients that query it, so GraphQL APIs deprecate fields and track usage instead of versioning URLs. And flexible queries move cost onto the server: a nested query can trigger thousands of database calls (the N+1 problem) unless resolvers batch, and public GraphQL APIs need query cost limits.
Retrying a POST is unsafe, so clients should never retry writes.

Retrying a non-idempotent POST can duplicate the effect, but never retrying means a timeout leaves the client not knowing whether the payment happened. Idempotency keys resolve the dilemma: the client sends a unique key with the request and reuses it on retries; the server stores the first result under that key and returns it for any retry. Stripe's API accepts idempotency keys on all POST requests for exactly this reason.
An API version number in the URL solves compatibility.

A /v2 prefix lets a provider make breaking changes without breaking /v1 users — but it bundles every change into one big migration that many clients never make, leaving the provider maintaining both versions indefinitely. Most breakage in practice comes from unintended changes within a version: a field that changes format, an error that changes status code. Compatibility is a discipline on every change; the version scheme only decides how deliberate breaking changes are delivered.
lab:
Goal: see three API design decisions in running code: the same response as JSON and as protobuf wire bytes (encoded by hand, so nothing is magic), offset versus cursor pagination while new rows arrive, and idempotency keys under retries. Stdlib only, Python 3.12, runs instantly.

  1. Save the script as swe7_lab.py and run python swe7_lab.py.
  2. Part 1 prints the invoice as 92 bytes of JSON and 25 bytes of protobuf, with the hex: 08 d5 f8 02 12 08 63 75 73 5f 39 66 32 6b 18 ec f6 07 22 03 45 55 52 28 02. Check it against the diagram: 08 is field 1, varint; d5 f8 02 decodes to 85 + 120×128 + 2×16,384 = 48,213.
  3. Part 2 fetches page 1 of ten orders, inserts two new orders, and fetches page 2 both ways. Offset returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 6] — orders 3 and 4 twice. Cursor returns [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8].
  4. Part 3 simulates a client whose first two responses are lost to timeouts, so it sends the same charge three times. Without an idempotency key the server creates 3 charges; with one key reused on every retry, it creates 1.

What to look for: in part 1, that field names never appear in the protobuf bytes — only numbers — which is why protobuf field numbers can never be reused. In part 3, that the key is generated once per logical operation, outside the retry loop; generating it inside the loop would defeat it.

Try next: (1) Add a sixth field, string memo = 6, and confirm an old reader could skip it: its tag byte 32 says "field 6, length-delimited", and the length tells the reader how many bytes to jump. (2) Change the server to reject a reused key whose amount differs, as Stripe does. (3) Delete two orders between pages instead of inserting and watch offset pagination skip rows.

"""swe7 lab: (1) one API response as JSON vs protobuf wire format, encoded by hand;
(2) offset vs cursor pagination while rows are being inserted; (3) idempotency keys under retries."""
import json
import uuid

# ---------- 1. JSON vs protobuf wire format ----------
# message Invoice { int64 id = 1; string customer_id = 2; int64 amount_cents = 3; string currency = 4; Status status = 5; }
invoice = {"id": 48213, "customer_id": "cus_9f2k", "amount_cents": 129900, "currency": "EUR", "status": "PAID"}
STATUS = {"DRAFT": 0, "OPEN": 1, "PAID": 2}

def varint(n: int) -> bytes:                      # 7 bits per byte, low bits first, high bit = "more bytes follow"
    out = bytearray()
    while True:
        b = n & 0x7F
        n >>= 7
        if n:
            out.append(b | 0x80)
        else:
            out.append(b)
            return bytes(out)

def field(num: int, value) -> bytes:
    if isinstance(value, int):                     # wire type 0 = varint
        return varint(num << 3 | 0) + varint(value)
    data = value.encode()                          # wire type 2 = length-delimited
    return varint(num << 3 | 2) + varint(len(data)) + data

pb = (field(1, invoice["id"]) + field(2, invoice["customer_id"]) + field(3, invoice["amount_cents"])
      + field(4, invoice["currency"]) + field(5, STATUS[invoice["status"]]))
js = json.dumps(invoice, separators=(",", ":")).encode()
print(f"JSON     {len(js):3} bytes  {js.decode()}")
print(f"protobuf {len(pb):3} bytes  {pb.hex(' ')}")
print(f"  id=48213 as varint: {varint(48213).hex(' ')}   (0xd5 0xf8 0x02 -> 0x55 + 0x78<<7 + 0x02<<14)")
assert varint(48213) == bytes([0xD5, 0xF8, 0x02]) and len(pb) == 25

# ---------- 2. offset vs cursor pagination while new rows arrive ----------
rows = [{"id": i, "created": 1000 - i} for i in range(1, 11)]        # newest first: id 1 is newest
def page_offset(data, offset, limit):
    return data[offset:offset + limit]
def page_cursor(data, after_id, limit):                               # "items older than the last one I saw"
    start = 0 if after_id is None else next(i for i, r in enumerate(data) if r["id"] == after_id) + 1
    page = data[start:start + limit]
    return page, (page[-1]["id"] if page else None)

seen_offset, seen_cursor = [], []
table = list(rows)
p1 = page_offset(table, 0, 4); seen_offset += [r["id"] for r in p1]
c1, cur = page_cursor(table, None, 4); seen_cursor += [r["id"] for r in c1]
table.insert(0, {"id": 99, "created": 2000}); table.insert(0, {"id": 98, "created": 2001})   # two new orders arrive
p2 = page_offset(table, 4, 4); seen_offset += [r["id"] for r in p2]
c2, cur = page_cursor(table, cur, 4); seen_cursor += [r["id"] for r in c2]
print(f"\noffset pages: {seen_offset}   duplicates: {sorted({i for i in seen_offset if seen_offset.count(i) > 1})}")
print(f"cursor pages: {seen_cursor}   duplicates: none")
assert seen_offset == [1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 6] and seen_cursor == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]

# ---------- 3. idempotency keys: a retry after a lost response must not charge twice ----------
class PaymentAPI:
    def __init__(self):
        self.charges, self.seen = [], {}
    def create_charge(self, amount_cents: int, idempotency_key: str | None = None) -> dict:
        if idempotency_key in self.seen:
            return self.seen[idempotency_key]          # replay the stored response, do nothing new
        charge = {"id": f"ch_{len(self.charges) + 1}", "amount": amount_cents}
        self.charges.append(charge)
        if idempotency_key:
            self.seen[idempotency_key] = charge
        return charge

def client_with_retry(api, amount, use_key: bool):
    key = str(uuid.uuid4()) if use_key else None        # ONE key per logical operation, reused on every retry
    for attempt in range(3):
        resp = api.create_charge(amount, key)
        if attempt < 2:
            continue                                   # simulate: response lost to a timeout, client retries
        return resp

for use_key in (False, True):
    api = PaymentAPI()
    client_with_retry(api, 4999, use_key)
    print(f"\nidempotency key={'yes' if use_key else 'no '}: charges created = {len(api.charges)}")
    assert len(api.charges) == (1 if use_key else 3)
recap: An API is a contract that other teams write code against; once one client depends on it, every observable behaviour becomes hard to change, so design deliberately and change compatibly.
Resource-oriented design names nouns (/invoices/{id}), uses standard methods with their HTTP semantics, and reserves custom methods for actions that don't fit create, read, update, delete.

Status codes tell clients what to do next — fix the request (4xx), retry later (429, 503 with Retry-After) or report a bug (500) — and error bodies should be machine-readable, for example RFC 9457 problem details with a stable error code.
Idempotency keys make non-idempotent operations safe to retry: the server stores the first response under the client's key and replays it for retries, comparing parameters to catch misuse.
Cursor (keyset) pagination returns items after the last one seen, so it neither duplicates nor skips rows when data changes between pages, unlike offset pagination.
Long-running work returns 202 Accepted with a status resource to poll or a webhook, rather than holding a request open.

Backward-compatible changes add optional things; breaking changes remove, rename, retype or change meaning; Stripe delivers breaking changes as small date-named versions, pins each account to the version of its first request, and transforms responses backwards through version-change modules.

REST over JSON is universal and cache-friendly, gRPC gives typed contracts, compact binary encoding, streaming and deadlines for service-to-service calls, and GraphQL lets clients choose fields at the cost of server-side query complexity.

LLM APIs apply the same principles: pinned model versions, schemas for tool calls and structured output, streaming responses, token-based rate limits, and idempotency for agent actions with side effects.
glossary: 202 Accepted
An HTTP status meaning the request was accepted for processing but hasn't completed; usually returned with the location of a status resource.
Backward-compatible change
A change to an API that existing clients keep working with, such as adding an optional field or a new endpoint.
Breaking change
A change that can make existing clients fail, such as removing or renaming a field, changing its type or meaning, or making an optional input required.
Cursor (keyset) pagination
Paging by passing an opaque token that identifies the last item seen, so the next page starts after it regardless of inserts or deletes.
Deadline
In gRPC, an absolute time by which a call must finish; it propagates to downstream calls so work stops when the caller has given up.
GraphQL
A query language and runtime for APIs in which clients send a query describing exactly the fields they want, served from one endpoint.
gRPC
A remote procedure call framework from Google that sends Protocol Buffers messages over HTTP/2, with generated clients and support for streaming.
Hyrum's law
The observation that with enough users, every observable behaviour of an API will be depended on by somebody, whatever the documented contract says.
Idempotency key
A unique value a client sends with a request and reuses on retries, so the server can recognise duplicates and return the original result.
Idempotent
An operation whose effect is the same whether performed once or many times; in HTTP, GET, PUT and DELETE are defined as idempotent, POST is not.
LLM (large language model)
A neural network that generates text from a prompt; LLM APIs stream tokens and version their models by date.
N+1 problem
Issuing one query to fetch a list and then one more query per item, so a page of 100 items costs 101 queries.
Offset pagination
Paging with ?offset=40&limit=20; simple, but pages shift when rows are inserted or deleted, causing duplicates or skips.
Problem details (RFC 9457)
A standard JSON format for HTTP API errors with type, title, status, detail and instance fields, plus extensions.
Protocol Buffers (protobuf)
Google's language-neutral schema language and compact binary encoding for structured data, in which fields are identified by numbers rather than names.
Resource
A named thing an API exposes, such as an invoice or a customer, identified by a URL and manipulated through standard methods.
REST
Representational State Transfer: an architectural style for networked APIs built on resources, standard methods, statelessness and cacheable representations.
Server-sent events (SSE)
A simple HTTP streaming format in which the server sends a sequence of text events over one long-lived response; widely used to stream LLM tokens.
Tolerant reader
A client that ignores fields and values it doesn't recognise, so providers can add them without breaking it.
UUID
Universally unique identifier: a 128-bit random or time-based value, commonly used for idempotency keys because collisions are practically impossible.
Varint
Protobuf's variable-length integer encoding: 7 bits per byte, with the high bit marking that more bytes follow, so small numbers take one byte.
Webhook
An HTTP callback: the provider sends a request to a URL the client registered when an event happens, instead of the client polling.
drill:
Design it

Design the API for creating a money transfer from a mobile app on flaky networks. Requirements: the user must never be charged twice; the app needs the transfer's final status, which can take up to a minute; users list their transfers newest first.

Answer 
POST /v1/transfers
Idempotency-Key: 7c1f…        (client-generated UUID per user action)
{ "from_account": "acc_1", "to_account": "acc_9", "amount": 2500, "currency": "GBP" }

202 Accepted
Location: /v1/transfers/tr_123
{ "id": "tr_123", "status": "pending", ... }

GET /v1/transfers/tr_123          -> 200 { "status": "completed" | "failed", "failure_reason": ... }
GET /v1/transfers?limit=20&after=<cursor>   -> newest first, keyset-paginated
  • Idempotency key generated once per tap, reused on every retry. The server stores key + request hash + response in the same transaction as creating the transfer; the same key and body return the original response; the same key with a different body returns 422; a retry while the first is still processing gets 409.
  • 202 + polling (or a webhook or push notification) because completion is asynchronous; never hold a request open for a minute. The transfer is a state machine: pending → completed | failed.
  • Amounts as integer minor units with a currency code, never floats; prefixed opaque IDs.
  • Errors as problem details with stable codes: 400 malformed, 401/403 auth, 404 unknown account (also for accounts the caller can't see), 409 conflict, 422 business rule (insufficient funds), 429 with Retry-After.
  • Cursor pagination on (created_at, id) because new transfers arrive constantly — offset paging would duplicate or skip rows.
  • Authorisation on every read: a transfer is visible only to its account's owner.
qa: E
What makes an API well designed?

It's consistent (the same patterns for naming, errors and pagination everywhere), predictable (standard methods and status codes mean what HTTP says they mean), hard to misuse (idempotent retries, explicit units, validation with clear errors), and evolvable (clients tolerate additions, and breaking changes are rare and deliberate). And it's designed from the client's use cases, not from the database schema.
E
What's the difference between PUT and PATCH, and which are idempotent?

PUT replaces the whole resource with the representation sent, so sending it twice leaves the same state — it's idempotent. PATCH applies a partial modification; whether it's idempotent depends on the patch: 'set email to x' is, 'append item' is not. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition; POST is not, which is why POST creates need idempotency keys for safe retries.
E
Which status codes would you use for validation errors, auth failures and rate limiting?

400 for a malformed request and 422 for a well-formed one that fails business rules (teams vary; be consistent). 401 when the caller isn't authenticated, 403 when authenticated but not allowed — or 404 if revealing the resource exists would leak information. 409 for a conflict with current state. 429 for rate limiting, with Retry-After. 5xx only for server faults, with 503 plus Retry-After for temporary overload.
M
How do idempotency keys work, and what are the edge cases?

The client generates a unique key per logical operation and sends it on the request and every retry. The server, atomically with performing the operation, stores the key with a hash of the request and the response; a retry with the same key and body returns the stored response without redoing the work. Edge cases: the same key with a different body should be rejected; a retry arriving while the first is still running should get a conflict or wait; keys need a retention window (Stripe allows pruning after 24 hours); and failures before execution begins shouldn't be stored, so they can be retried.
Follow-up: where does the key get stored? — In the same database transaction as the side effect, so a crash can't record one without the other.
M
Why prefer cursor pagination over offset pagination?

Offset pagination counts rows from the start, so if rows are inserted or deleted between page requests, pages shift: new rows at the top push already-seen rows onto the next page (duplicates) and deletions pull unseen rows back (skips). It's also slow for deep pages, because the database must scan and discard all skipped rows. A cursor encodes the position of the last item seen (for example its created_at and id), and the next query asks for items after it using an index, which is stable and fast at any depth.
M
What changes are backward compatible, and which are breaking?

Compatible: adding a new endpoint, adding an optional request parameter, adding a response field (for tolerant readers), relaxing a validation. Breaking: removing or renaming a field, changing a type or format, changing a default, making an optional parameter required, tightening validation, changing an error code or status, and changing semantics while keeping the shape. Adding an enum value is compatible only if clients were told to handle unknown values.
Follow-up: how do you catch accidental breaking changes? — Diff the API schema (OpenAPI or protobuf) in CI with a breaking-change checker, and run consumer contract tests against the provider.
M
How does Stripe version its API?

With small, date-named versions such as 2017-05-24 rather than big v1/v2 releases. An account is pinned to the latest version on its first request and stays there until it upgrades; any request can override with a Stripe-Version header. Internally, responses are built at the current version and then transformed backwards through a list of version-change modules until they match the requested version, so old versions don't clutter core code. Stripe reported maintaining compatibility with every version since 2011, through almost a hundred breaking changes in six years.
M
When would you choose gRPC, REST or GraphQL?

REST/JSON for public APIs and anything browsers or third parties call — universal tooling, HTTP caching, easy debugging. gRPC for internal service-to-service calls where you control both ends and want a typed contract, generated clients, streaming and deadline propagation, and efficiency at high request rates. GraphQL when many client types (web, mobile, partners) need different shapes of related data from one backend and round trips are costly, accepting the server-side cost controls it needs.
M
How should an API report errors?

With the right status class so generic clients and proxies behave correctly, and a machine-readable body with a stable error code clients can branch on, a human-readable message, and the field at fault for validation errors. RFC 9457 problem details (application/problem+json) standardises the shape. Never leak stack traces or internal details, include a request ID for support, and keep error codes as stable as any other part of the contract.
H
Encode the same small response in JSON and in protobuf and explain the size difference.

The invoice {id: 48213, customer_id: 'cus_9f2k', amount_cents: 129900, currency: 'EUR', status: PAID} is 92 bytes of compact JSON. In protobuf each field is a tag byte (field number shifted left 3 bits, plus a wire type) and a value: id is 08 then the varint d5 f8 02; the string is 12, a length 08 and eight bytes; amount 18 ec f6 07; currency 22 03 'EUR'; status 28 02 — 25 bytes total. The savings come from numeric field tags instead of repeated names, varints instead of decimal text, and enums as small integers; the cost is that the bytes are meaningless without the schema.

Follow-up: what does this imply for schema evolution? — Field numbers are the contract, so they must never be reused or changed; removed fields are marked reserved, and renaming a field is safe on the wire but breaks JSON mappings and generated code.
H
Design an API for a long-running operation, such as fine-tuning a model or generating a report.

POST /fine-tuning-jobs with an idempotency key returns 202 Accepted and a job resource {id, status: queued}. Clients poll GET /fine-tuning-jobs/{id} with backoff, or register a webhook to be notified; the job has explicit states (queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled) and a cancel method. Results are separate resources referenced from the finished job. List endpoints use cursor pagination. Progress events can be streamed, but the job must survive the client disconnecting.

Follow-up: how do you make webhooks reliable? — Sign them, retry with backoff until acknowledged, include an event ID so receivers deduplicate, and offer an events list endpoint so receivers can catch up after downtime.
H
What is Hyrum's law and how does it affect API evolution?

With enough users, every observable behaviour of an API will be depended on by somebody, regardless of the documented contract — ordering of results, error message text, timing, default page size. So changes that are 'compatible' by the contract can still break real clients. Defences: document and randomise behaviours you don't promise (for example, don't return results in an accidental order), make error codes rather than messages the contract, measure what clients actually use, and roll out even compatible changes gradually with monitoring.
H
What API design issues are specific to LLM-backed services?

Model output is streamed, so APIs use server-sent events or gRPC streaming, with a final event carrying usage and a stop reason. Models change behaviour between versions, so clients pin dated model versions and providers deprecate them on a schedule, much like Stripe's API versions. Tool calls and structured outputs are contracts defined by JSON schemas, versioned like any API. Rate limits are in tokens as well as requests. And agents calling APIs with side effects need idempotency keys and confirmation steps, because a model may repeat an action after a timeout.

Stripe, 2017 — why retries need idempotency keys and how the server should handle them.
The contract in practice: stored first response, parameter comparison, 24-hour pruning.
